Name: depth_budget_truncation
Title: Running Out of Layers: Cross-Lingual Errors as Truncated Concept Computation Under a Fixed Depth Budget
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs allocate the same fixed number of layers to every language, but low-resource and typologically distant languages require MORE layers to finish computing a concept; consequently their concept computation is frequently TRUNCATED by the fixed depth budget before it converges, and this truncation — not missing knowledge — causes a large fraction of cross-lingual errors. The required-depth deficit scales with typological/script distance and resource level, and errors are causally recoverable by granting extra late-layer compute (looping late layers) without any retraining.
Related Work: Probing work shows concepts become decodable at different depths depending on complexity ('Concept Depth' 2024) and that low-resource languages exhibit flatter, shallower layer-wise probing trends than high-resource ones (Cross-Language Probing 2024), and that difficulty is encoded language-agnostically early then language-specifically late ('Shared Geometry of Difficulty' 2026). Cross-Layer Transcoder and latent-language work localize a shared middle-layer space with lossy late-layer decoding (Tracing Multilingual Representations 2025; MALT 2025), and DAMA (2026) reports a U-shaped adaptability pattern in speech ASR. ALL of these are correlational (where a concept is decodable, how well probes align by layer) or propose fine-tuning/adaptation fixes. NONE reframes the layer-wise gap as a CAUSAL compute-deadline problem: that the fixed layer budget TRUNCATES an in-progress concept computation for languages that need more depth, that this truncation (not absent knowledge) is what produces the error, or that granting extra inference-time depth to just those items causally recovers the answer. We contribute this compute-budget-truncation reframing, a per-item 'required depth' measurement, a causal early-exit/late-layer-looping test, and a training-free depth-budget intervention. We separate a causal THEORY (the fixed depth budget truncates unfinished concept computation for depth-hungry languages, and truncation - not missing knowledge - causes the error) from an ENGINEERING intervention (late-layer looping). The primary novelty is the causal theory and its per-item required-depth estimand; the looping fix is a corollary probe reported with its costs. The boundary against Concept Depth and cross-language probing is sharp: those localize WHERE a concept becomes decodable but never causally attribute errors to insufficient depth. Unlike general reasoning-loop papers, the multilingual case supplies a natural, non-engineered source of variation in required depth (language distance) and a matched-item control (the same fact in a shallow-converging language).
Abstract: Multilingual language models answer questions far more reliably in high-resource, typologically close languages, and interpretability work has shown that concepts become decodable at different layer depths across languages. But this has been treated as a correlational fact about representation geometry. We propose a causal, resource-based reframing: transformers apply a fixed number of layers to every input, yet distant, low-resource languages need MORE layers to finish computing a concept, so their computation is often truncated by the depth budget before it converges — the model 'runs out of layers.' Under this view, many cross-lingual errors are not missing knowledge but unfinished computation. We measure, per item and per language, the 'required depth' at which the correct answer first stabilizes via logit-lens/early-exit trajectories, and define a Truncation Gap as the fraction of items whose answer converges only in layers deeper than the model has, or would if given more. We test three claims: (1) required depth is systematically greater for distant/low-resource languages on identical facts, and the excess predicts errors; (2) errors on truncated items are causally distinguished from knowledge failures — early-exiting a high-resource run at the low-resource run's shallower effective depth reproduces the error, and, crucially, granting extra late-layer compute (looping the final transformer layers) at inference recovers correct answers specifically on high-required-depth items; and (3) the required-depth deficit and recovery scale with typological/script distance and resource level. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA factual QA and MGSM reasoning across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The work recasts the multilingual gap as a depth-budget truncation phenomenon with a cheap, training-free inference-time fix. Practically, adaptive per-item depth allocation trades a little extra late-layer compute for recovered low-resource accuracy - a favorable latency/compute tradeoff we quantify as accuracy gained per extra layer-pass and cost per recovered answer - so deployment teams could route only high-required-depth items to extra compute. We state expectations as preregistered effect-size ranges with confidence intervals rather than hard cutoffs, and validate on a translation task in addition to factual QA and reasoning.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Data (existing, used as is): parallel factual QA from mLAMA/BMLAMA-53 (1,000 facts present in all chosen languages) and multilingual grade-school math from MGSM (250 problems; its 10-11 languages for the reasoning arm), so the SAME item is posed in every language. Languages span Latin/Cyrillic/Perso-Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. Models of differing depth (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference only, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B (32 layers), Aya-23-8B (32 layers), Qwen2-7B (28 layers). Layer-wise readout by logit lens and a tuned lens (the lens's affine map is the only trained parameter, per layer). Per-language typological/script distance from lang2vec; resource proxy from CC-100. Answer matching alias-aware, last-token/answer-span. 3 seeds (item sampling).

Experiment 1 (H1 - distant/low-resource languages need more layers for the same concept). Tests whether required depth is systematically greater for distant/low-resource languages on IDENTICAL facts. For each (item, language) record the CONVERGENCE DEPTH: the shallowest layer after which the top-ranked answer token becomes and stays correct through the final layer (stability judged over the last several layers). Decisive metric: mean convergence depth per language on the shared item set, compared across the resource/distance groups. Convincing: distant/low-resource languages have mean convergence depth deeper than close/high-resource ones by >= 3 layers on the same facts, consistently across models. Indecision band: 1-3 layers deeper; reported as a weak depth shift. Negative result: convergence depth not deeper for distant languages (< 1 layer) refutes H1.

Experiment 2 (H3 - required-depth deficit scales with distance and resource). Tests whether the depth deficit tracks typological/script distance and resource level. Define per-language mean required depth and the TRUNCATION GAP = fraction of items whose answer converges only in the last few layers or is still rising/unconverged at the final layer (right-censored). Correlate both with lang2vec distance and the resource proxy; designed contrast: a distant-but-well-covered language vs a close-but-sparse one to partly separate the axes. Decisive metric: Spearman of required depth / Truncation Gap with distance and with resource (95% CIs). Convincing: both correlate (Spearman >= 0.4) with distance and with resource. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4; reported as suggestive. Negative result: no correlation (< 0.2) refutes H3.

Experiment 3 (H2 - shallow budget causally reproduces the low-resource error). Tests whether truncation, not missing knowledge, causes the error. Take facts answered CORRECTLY in a high-resource language with convergence depth d_hi; force EARLY EXIT of the high-resource run at the shallower effective depth d_lo observed for a low-resource language and test whether the high-resource answer degrades to the low-resource-style error. Specificity: early-exiting at d_hi should not degrade. Model frozen; early exit via the tuned lens at inference. Decisive metric: degradation rate induced by early exit at d_lo (reported first), with the d_hi early-exit degradation as the specificity floor. Convincing: early exit at d_lo degrades >= 50% of previously-correct high-resource answers while early exit at d_hi degrades < 10%. Indecision band: 25-50% degradation at d_lo; reported as partial support for the budget account. Negative result: < 25% degradation (shallow budget alone does not reproduce the error) refutes the truncation-causes-error claim.

Experiment 4 (H2 - truncation-type vs knowledge-type errors dissociate). Tests the crucial separation between unfinished computation and absent knowledge. Partition low-resource errors into TRUNCATION-type (the fact is answered correctly in the high-resource language, so the knowledge exists; the low-resource error co-occurs with a late/unconverged trajectory) vs KNOWLEDGE-type (wrong in the high-resource language too). Model frozen. Decisive metric: the difference in late-layer-looping recovery (from Exp. 5) between truncation-type and knowledge-type errors; here we first establish the partition sizes and that trajectory lateness predicts truncation-type membership. Convincing: truncation-type errors are a substantial share (>= 30% of low-resource errors) and are marked by significantly later/unconverged trajectories than knowledge-type errors. Indecision band: truncation-type 15-30%; reported as a smaller-than-claimed contribution. Negative result: truncation-type < 15% or trajectory lateness not distinguishing the two types refutes the truncation-vs-knowledge dissociation central to H2.

Experiment 5 (H4 - extra late-layer compute recovers truncated answers, training-free). Tests whether granting extra depth by LOOPING the final k transformer layers at inference recovers correct answers specifically on high-required-depth (truncation-type) items. Feed the last block's residual stream back through the last k blocks one or more times on the low-resource/distant run; dose-response over loop iterations and over k (last-1 vs last-k). Model frozen; no weights changed. Compare against a naive "add CoT tokens" baseline, translate-to-English, and a control that loops RANDOM blocks. Decisive metric: accuracy gain on high-Truncation-Gap items (reported first), split by error type, with output-language fidelity, fluency (perplexity), and specificity (already-converged items unchanged) alongside. Convincing: late-layer looping recovers >= 15 pp on truncation-type items, near-zero (< 5 pp) on knowledge-type items and on already-converged items, exceeds the random-block control, with a coherent dose-response and < 5% perplexity change. Indecision band: 5-15 pp recovery on truncation-type items, or recovery not concentrated on them; reported as a weak/ambiguous fix, while Exp. 1-4 (correlational required-depth + causal early-exit) still stand. Negative result: < 5 pp recovery or looping helping knowledge-type/converged items equally (i.e., generic corruption/help) refutes H4.

Computation-vs-rescoring controls and translation task. To test whether looping recovers answers via deeper COMPUTATION rather than mere answer-token re-scoring, Experiment 5 adds (i) a MATCHED-DEPTH RECOMPUTATION control (tuned-lens continuation for the same number of extra passes) and (ii) a logit-renormalization/temperature control that re-ranks final logits without extra computation; recovery must exceed both and the random-block control. We add a multilingual TRANSLATION subset (FLORES-200 sentence pairs) so the depth-budget account is tested on a generation task, and we validate required-depth measurements with a tuned lens plus a hidden-state perturbation test, defining required depth via a stability (not first-crossing) criterion with right-censoring for non-converging trajectories. All hard thresholds are reported as preregistered effect-size ranges with confidence intervals.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Logit-lens convergence depth can reflect the readout basis rather than genuine computation state; we validate with a tuned lens and require the causal early-exit (Exp. 5) and late-layer-looping (Exp. 6) results to promote the depth measurement to a functional claim. 2. Late-layer looping is an untied-weights hack the model was not trained for and may simply corrupt representations rather than 'continue' computation; we mitigate by reporting dose-response, specificity (already-converged items must be unharmed), and by comparing looping the last block vs random blocks; if looping helps only on high-required-depth truncation-type items and not on knowledge-type or converged items, that pattern is strong evidence regardless of the hack's crudeness. A negative looping result still leaves the correlational required-depth + causal early-exit findings intact. 3. Truncation and knowledge failure are entangled; the high-resource-language knowledge control (Exp. 7) is the crucial dissociator and central to the claim. 4. Distance and resource level are correlated; the dissociating language contrasts (Exp. 4) only partly separate them, and we report multiple resource proxies. 5. Right-censored (unconverged) trajectories are hard to distinguish from noise; we use stability criteria over the last several layers and report robustness to the convergence definition. 6. Answer matching across scripts is noisy; we use alias-aware, last-token/answer-span matching and report tokenization statistics. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families of differing depth address but do not exhaust generality, and the model-depth ablation directly tests the budget interpretation.
